Actual Article Body:
A portion of an FBI affidavit supporting a criminal complaint against Ian Brinksman, a federal contractor in Washington, D.C., charged on Oct. 23, 2026, with leaking classified information to a reporter.

The FBI on Oct. 23, 2026, arrested Washington, D.C.-based government contractor Ian Brinksman and charged him with leaking classified national defense information to a reporter.

Authorities charged Brinksman, who had a top-secret security clearance, with unlawfully transmitting the information in violation of the Espionage Act. They allege he repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports outside his work duties and shared information with a journalist he knew intended to publish it.

According to a Justice Department press release, Brinksman began working for a U.S. government agency in 2020, before becoming a systems integration developer for a private contractor serving the same agency in 2022. The release also said Brinksman provided services to the CIA.

Authorities, who searched his Washington, D.C., home before his arrest, allege Brinksman accessed five classified reports between March and October 2026 that fell outside the scope of his work. They allege he also communicated with a journalist he was romantically involved with around the time he viewed them.

An FBI affidavit identifies the journalist only as “Individual 1.” It cites a September 2026 fundraising post by a Substack outlet in which the reporter said she had published reporting based on classified assessments from the agency where Brinksman worked.

A Sept. 28 post by Aída Chávez, who publishes the Substack newsletter Capital & Empire, contains the same statement, “Over the past year, I’ve published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about.” Capital & Empire did not respond to a request for comment.

The affidavit alleges the journalist published at least five articles containing information that matched classified reports Brinksman accessed, some marked “top secret.” It cites phone records, database logs, building access records and emails as evidence.

Brinksman was one of no more than six people who accessed the Substack page from the government facility between March and October 2026, according to the affidavit. He was the only one investigators identified as having accessed all five reports and viewed all five articles.

The affidavit also describes Brinksman and “Individual 1” exchanging edits on a Google document about geopolitical issues in the Middle East before an article on the subject was published. Investigators said they had not identified classified information in that article.

In a Nov. 20, 2025, email to a friend, Brinksman described helping a journalist he was dating launch an independent foreign policy publication. “I’m getting a surprising amount enrichment/fulfilment from working on that,” he wrote, according to the affidavit.

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that protecting U.S. secrets was a top counterintelligence priority. “Anyone caught abusing their position of trust within the government by jeopardizing national security and putting our brave warriors at risk will be met with the full weight of justice.”
